gloss: In the inscriptions of the famous Udayagiri near Vidisha we see Atrakakardava, commander of Chandragupta II Vikramaditya, making such a donation to the Kakanadabota (old name of Sanchi) mahavihara. In Kumaragupta's time royal patronage had a role in establishing a mahavihara and university like Nalanda, which Harsha extended by donating several hundred villages. Not only Nalanda, many other world-famous institutions of that era depended on land grants, from Vallabhi in the west to the Big Temple of the Chola kings in the south. These grants were called agrahara (to scholars or persons of religious importance), devadeya or mathapura.
note: Precedents of royal land grants to monasteries: the Udayagiri inscriptions near Vidisha record Chandragupta II's commander giving such a grant to the Kakanadabota (Sanchi) mahavihara; Nalanda, Harsha and other institutions depended on such grants.

gloss: Looking at the vastness and grandeur of Udaypur, its budget must have been quite large from its economic and administrative side. Since Udayaditya was the ruler, resources for the temple must certainly have been arranged through such grants. No inscription giving detailed information on this has been found. If one is ever found, it may help in understanding the temple's economy.
note: Author's inference that Udaypur temple must have had a good budget with resources arranged by grants under Udayaditya; no inscription giving details has been found.

segments: इस अभिलेख पर तिथि संवत् 1286 (1229 ईस्वी) कार्तिक सुदि...शुक्रवार लिखी है। तिथि का अंतिम भाग टूटा हुआ है। इस अभिलेख का मकसद महाराजा देवपालदेव के शासनकाल में राजकोष अधिकारी धामदेव द्वारा उदयेश्वरदेव के मंदिर के निमित्त 4 बिस्वा भूमि के दान का उल्लेख करना है।
gloss: The date on this inscription is written Samvat 1286 (1229 CE) Kartik sudi ... Friday. The last part of the date is broken. The purpose of this inscription is to mention the donation of 4 biswa of land for the temple of Udayeshvaradeva by Dhamadeva, treasury officer, during the reign of Maharaja Devapaladeva.
note: Dated VS 1286 (1229 CE), Kartik sudi, Friday (date end broken); records a gift of 4 biswa of land to the Udayeshvaradeva temple by treasury officer Dhamadeva in the reign of Maharaja Devapaladeva.

quote: संभव है आकार में बहुत छोटे नजर आने वाले जमीन के इस टुकड़े की कुछ खासियत रही हो। वह जल के स्रोत से परिपूर्ण हो ताकि इस मंदिर के लिए जलापूर्ति भली भांति सुनिश्चित की जा सके। वह राजपुरोहित या मुख्य प्रबंधक के आवासीय उपयोग के लिए दी गई थी या उस पर कोई शानदार बावड़ी थी, जिसका जल गर्भगृह में पूजा, अभिषेक या अनुष्ठानों के लिए विशेष रूप से संरक्षित किया गया हो! अगर इतनी सी जमीन का जिक्र इतने विशाल मंदिर पर अंकित किया गया है तो उसका इस्तेमाल भी बहुत ही खास किस्म का ही होना चाहिए था।
segments: संभव है आकार में बहुत छोटे नजर आने वाले जमीन के इस टुकड़े की कुछ खासियत रही हो। वह जल के स्रोत से परिपूर्ण हो ताकि इस मंदिर के लिए जलापूर्ति भली भांति सुनिश्चित की जा सके। वह राजपुरोहित या मुख्य प्रबंधक के आवासीय उपयोग के लिए दी गई थी या उस पर कोई शानदार बावड़ी थी, जिसका जल गर्भगृह में पूजा, अभिषेक या अनुष्ठानों के लिए विशेष रूप से संरक्षित किया गया हो! अगर इतनी सी जमीन का जिक्र इतने विशाल मंदिर पर अंकित किया गया है तो उसका इस्तेमाल भी बहुत ही खास किस्म का ही होना चाहिए था।
gloss: It is possible that this plot, small in size, had some special quality. It may have been full of water sources so that water supply for this temple could be ensured. It may have been given for the residential use of the royal priest or chief manager, or there may have been a splendid stepwell on it whose water was specially reserved for worship, abhisheka or rituals in the sanctum. If mention of so little land is inscribed on such a huge temple, its use too must have been of a very special kind.
note: Author's conjecture on why 4 biswa was notable: it may have had a water source for the temple's water supply, been a residence for the chief priest or manager, or held a fine stepwell whose water was reserved for the sanctum; not stated in the source inscription.

quote: To the pilgrim and devotee who goes to the temple, it is a Tirtha made by art, as others are by nature, and often it is both in one. A Hindu temple unlike the Vedic altar does not fulfil its purpose by being built; it has of necessity to be seen. Darsana, the looking at the temple, the seat, abode and body of divinity and its worship (pūjā), are the purpose of visiting the temple. To fulfil this purpose in addition to being an offering and work of pious liberality the temple has not only its proportionate measurement but also the carvings on its walls, and the total fact of its form.

images, must have received a fatal blow so that these craftsmen were now forced to orientate their craft to some other direction.
note: Stone carving in northern Madhya Bharat, the craft of the Patharphod, was occupied by medieval temple building and dealt a blow with the advent of Islam.

quote: Closely connected with the temples, there were many Vaishnava and Saiva mathams which were both teaching institutions and their educative influence was very great, especially in the Vedas and Sastras and the Puranas. The 'mathams', were important religious institutions They were encouraged by the State and possessed a vast amount of wealth'. There was a religious head for each 'matham' who was highly respected. Generally, every matham stood for the propagation of a particular school or religion and encouraged teaching and the spreading of knowledge in religious lore. quote: The Mathas of southern India were extraordinary multi-purpose institutions. On one hand, they were educational institutes attached to temples, in which monks and students lived together. On the other, they served as rest houses for travellers including pilgrims and musicians, and gave food to anyone who walked in. Some of them had hospitals to take care of the sick. There are inscriptions indicating that even sick animals were treated in some Mathas by physicians trained in veterinary medicine. The monks who taught here were well-versed in various branches of learning. Many Mathas were equipped with libraries and preserved manuscripts. Thus, these public institutions rendered a variety of services while promoting learning. They were funded by kings or communities or philanthropists.

quote: The Spirit behind remunerating the pujari as recommended in the agama is one of honoring and making happy rather than payment for his service. In Vastudevabali, the acharyalaksana specifies that the acharya should be happy and content and honoured with dakshina. In fact, here the agama is quite visual in its description and brings forth a scenario of the acharya seated on an appropriate seat, wearing all five specified ornaments, with all five specified ornaments, with a headgear and topcloth, surrounded by similarly attired murtipas accompanied by the chanting of veda, storta and mantra. He has been properly honoured with dakshina, to gladden his heart. In the Vyadhinasanavidanavidhi, the adisaiva officiant who conducts the prescribed ritual for either healing or protection is to be honoured with appropriate dakshina, to gladden his heart. The agama declares that if the acarya is happy, everything moving and stationary becomes happy.

quote: One of the Tiruvorriyur inscriptions states that as many as 60 velis were given for the maintenance of a mandapa built in the temple, for the upkeep of the teachers and pupils who studied grammar in that hall, and, for the worship of the god Sivadharman and Siddhanta were also taught. In a stone inscription from the Venkatesa Perumal temple at Tirumukkudal near Conjeevaram it is stated that besides a hospital, the temple maintained a hostel and college. An epigraph' of the time of Rajendara Chola I at Ennayiram (South Arcot District) gives many interesting details to show that temples of South India served the purpose of educational institutions. This inscription is of great importance for it shows clearly that in ancient temples not only was the regular conducting of worship maintained but also the study of the Vedas, philosophy, grammar and other sciences, and in a few cases, provision was made for a few persons versed in the Vedas.

quote: From inscription it appears that a lucrative prasadam trade began in the mandir as the quantity of daily offerings returned to the donor and the mandir functionaries far exceeded what could be consumed by them. Pilgrims visiting the mandir also desired to receive the prasadam for themselves and their family members who could not attend the mandir. From inscriptional evidence, it appears mandir functionaries and donors would turn their prasadam shares over to a group of 11 vendors (prasadakkar) who would subsequently sell the prasadam to visiting pilgrims. On average, it appears that a typical donation would return a total annual return of \(10\%\) (split as described above: \(25\%\) to the donor and \(75\%\) to mandir functionaries). The prasadakkar would pay a lease fee to the mandir functionary or donor in exchange for the ability to sell the prasadam to pilgrims at a profit. Based on inscriptions designating the right of the donor to transfer their prasadam share to a prasadakkarar, the prasadam trade was not illegal nor did it have negative connotations.

quote:
They constructed new mandirs and maintained surviving mandirs.
"Innumerable inscriptions from Chola times tell us of the philanthropy of the devadasis. They created new shrines, rebuilt old and crumbling ones, plated some of the roofs with cooper, gold, and brass. They commissioned master sculptors to make gold and bronze idols of gods, goddesses, and saints to be installed in mandirs. To conduct the worship of these idols, they also gifted rice and paddy. Part of their devadana was agricultural land. Sometimes they donated entire villages to make sure that the mandir was well maintained. Devadasis who had specific roles to play in the festivals and processions of mandirs donated lands to ensure the continuation of these celebrations. The wealthier devadasis donated jewels, lamps, plates, and bells made of slid gold for mandir service. To ensure that lamps remained perpetually lit in mandirs, they donated lands which yielded crops. Whenever natural calamities like cyclones and storms damaged mandir goruprams devadasis contributed money for their reconstruction. Their generosity extended to feeding brahmins and pilgrims.

quote: This was however a general nomenclature with a much wider connotation covering a variety of skills and occupations besides the conventional handicraft. In fact, in its first appearance, in the Brahmanas, it stands for works of art. In the Kausitaki Brahmana the term is extended even further to cover dance, drama and music. Silpa has also been defined in some texts as synonymous with the Vedic concept of karu a term which stands for a 'maker', covering a wide range of performers, an artisan, a singer, a poet. No difference or distinction was made between the various forms of expression and embraced a wide range of skilled activity from music to horsemanship, painting to cookery, weaving to magic show, all being regarded as equal. In course of time this acceptance of all creative force as an integrated power emerging from a single source, became defied as Viswakarma - the maker of the universe. The making of things was therefore a noble act, the object a manifestation of Viswakarma. The tradition, thus, grew of offering a light and flowers to Viswakarma or a deity with a prayer before starting on any operation by a craftsman, for it was an offering to the deity as a sign that he, the worker-maker, was going to enter into communion with the divine spirit.

quote: Founded in 972, the Lakulisha Temple at Ekalingaji (District Udaipur) is a large but simple structure, comprising a pancha-ratha sanctum, vestibule, closed hall with latticed windows in the lateral transepts and porch enclosed by a balustrade. The socle mouldings are simple and the wall is plain, but for two niches in the facade, one inset with an inscribed slab and the other with an image of Sarasvati. The brickwork super-structures of the shrine and the hall have practically crumbled. The sanctum enshrines an image of seated Lakulisha and the sanctum door-frame, showing 2 bands, displays an image of Lakulisha as the tutelary deity, surmounted by 5 niches containing figures of Ganesha, Brahma, Shiva, Vishnu and Karttikeya.

quote: With this object in view he set off from his capital, halting on his way at the present site of Udayapur at that time only a tiny village. Here he was sleeping in his tent, watched over by the queen, when another snake, which was guarding a treasure in a hole under a tree near by, peeped out to see what was happening. The first snake saw this and thereupon addressed the second from the stomach of the king, warning it that it would at once die, if anyone were to pour oil down into its hole. The treasure-guardian grew very angry, and retorted that the other snake was in no very safe position itself, since if anyone administered to the king a dose of pepper, salt, and buttermilk, that would be sufficient to put an end to its life.

quote:
Tradition gives a legendary story in connection with the establishment of this city. It runs as follows:—
One day the king, in the course of a hunting excursion, came upon a snake surrounded by fire and writhing in agony. He rescued the reptile, which at once begged for a drink of water. This being unobtainable, the king on the earnest request of the snake, put its mouth into his own in order to afford it temporary relief from its pain. But the snake betrayed his trust and slipped down into his stomach, which so upset and distressed the king that he determined to pass the rest of his life in Benares.

quote: A proverb about his valour is famous: "Where is King Bhoj, and where is Gangu the oilman!" (*Kान राजा भोज ने कान गंगू तेली*). In princely Malwi it is said thus: *"Kathe Raja Bhoj ne kathe Gangu Teli."* The root of this proverb is in fact in accord with history. In the above proverb, the *teli* (oilman) is also called *telan* (oil-woman): *"Kathe Raja Bhoj ne kathe Gangi Telan."* This reading of the proverb is closer to its origin, because King Bhoj's contemporary Gangeyadeva Kalachuri is known. The folk turned Gangeyadeva into "Gangi"; and turned "Telang" into "Telan." Thus Gangeyadeva Telang became Gangi Telan.

quote: For example, the Muslim sources inform us that he was alive in the following year, i.e., in 1233-34 A.C., when Sultân Ilutumish of Delhi made a heavy raid on Mâlwâ, capturing the fort of Bhilsâ (Vidishâ), and rushed so far as Ujjain where he demolished the temple of Mahâkâla and devastated the surrounding region.² That Dêvapâla was alive even thereafter when he revived the situation is known from the Mândhâtâ grant of the time of his son Jayavarman II, which states that the former killed a Muslim governor (Mlêchchhâdhipa) at Bhilsâ (Bhillasvâmipura),³ suggesting his reoccupation of the place. And that this locality continued to be in the possession of the Paramâras during the reign of Jayavarman (II) is also known from two inscriptions—one from Bhilsâ itself, dated V. 1320 (1263 A.C.) and the other, dated V. 1326 (1269 A.C.) from Pathâri, which is only about 55 kms. further north by east of the place.¹

quote: We know that in 1233-34 A.C. Ilutumish, the Turkish Sultān of Delhi, had turned his arms against Mālwā, where he captured the fort of Bhilsā (modern Vidishā) and from there he marched to Ujjain where he destroyed the temple of Mahākāla. \( ^{2} \)  These aggressive operations, though of a temporary nature, \( ^{3} \)  had opened a way for the Muslims to make expeditions further in the south; and during the years that followed, Nāsiruddīn's general Balban successfully over-ran the land up to Chanderī and Narwar which were then on the northern fringe of the Paramāra dominions. It was about in 1250 A.C.; \( ^{4} \)  and almost at the same time, that this region was attacked from the south by the Yādava Krishna, whose enmity with the house of the Paramāras was hereditary and who claims success over the contemporary king of Mālava in his epigraphical records. \( ^{5} \)  Almost about the same time the vāghelā Visaladēva of Gujarāt sacked Dhārā. \( ^{6} \)  And it is possible to hold that in view of all these troubles Jayavarman or his predecessor Jaitugi may have thought it best to resort to the fort of Māndū, which is a place of better strategic position than Dhārā, situated on the plains.

quote: He is said to have vanquished his enemies and firmly established dharmu; but the information furnished by the last of these verses is historically important, telling us that he “by his sword, cut off into two (the body of) the arrogant lord of the Mlechchhas, in a battle fought near Bhillasvāmipura,” which is Bhilsā, now known as Vidishā. This statement appears to have an allusion to the invasion of the city of Bhilsā by Iltutmish, the Turkish Sultān of Delhi. We know from the Muslim historians that this ruler subjugated the fort of Gwālior, in 632 A.H., or 1233-34 A.C., and soon after, advancing further in the south, he demolished the temple of Bhillasvāmin (at Bhilsā). \( ^{4} \)  But in view of the statement of the inscription under study, it would appear that Dēvapāla succeeded in recapturing the fort at the city, which remained in the possession of the Paramāras about half a century, till it was again snatched from them by the Khalji Sultāns of Delhi.

quote: \( ^{3} \)  From the Ujjain stone inscription of the Chaulukya Jayasimha of V.S. 1195 or 1138 A.C., we know that this king (Jayasimha) claims to be Avanti-nātha, which shows that he had conquered and annexed the whole of the Paramāra kingdom to the Chaulukya empire. \( ^{3} \)  This incident took place about fifteen years earlier than the time when the image bearing the present inscription was set up; and during the reign of Jayasimha's successor Kumārapāla (c. 1143-1172 A.C.) there was practically no change in the situation. quote:
This jaredari system gradually went into disuse after the
death of Maharaja Jankoji Rao (1827-1843), when the Council of Regency was set up and the zamindari system took its place. Henceforth, the land management of big villages was given on contract to land-holders. They were not only required to credit annually the Government demand, but were also required to furnish a rough account of the recoveries made from the cultivators. Lands cultivated by the contractors (Khud-kasht) were not assessed. On the expiry of the period of a particular lease, it was given to the same holder as far as possible.
In 1853, the jiarcdari system was abolished and leases for a term of 12 years were granted.

quote: In Gwalior State, Vidisha (Bhilsa) was a tahsil of Isagarh pargana. In 1904 Vidisha was raised to a District having two tahsils of Vidisha and Basoda till the formation of Madhya Bharat in 1948. The District was enlarged in 1949 by the merger of small States of Kurwai, Mohammadgarh and Pathari which formed Kurwai Tahsil. The Sironj sub-division with two tahsils of Sironj and Lateri, formerly in Kota district of Rajasthan State, and the small Pargana of Piklon consisting of 11 villages belonging to Bhopal State were added to the District in 1956 with the formation of new Madhya Pradesh. At the same time the town and the District were renamed as Vidisha.

quote: The development of irrigation in the former Gwalior State started with the accession of the princely ruler Madho Rao Scindia. There was a devastating famine in 1898 and again in 1900, and the Ruler decided to constitute a special Irrigation Department in the year 1905. He was keen to get the minor irrigation works constructed in all districts of the State. This policy was followed by the Irrigation Department of the State till 1914. The genesis of irrigation thus lay in the distress caused by famines.

quote: Given the inextricable connection between a monarch and his royal temple, the inverted funnel through which power flowed down to him, it is not surprising that temple desecration became an act with which to set the seal on a conquest. Often this meant carrying home the principal idol, or it could be a matter of destroying the main shrine or even the entire temple. Later temple destruction by Muslims was largely a continuation of this tradition, rather than iconoclasm.

quote: The light shed, from the 1950s onwards, by Indian Marxist-inspired historians applying the model of feudalism to medieval India, was more penetrating. According to their analysis, the contraction of long-distance trade led to the decline of cities, of artisanal production, of a money economy and centralised taxation. Kings had to resort to land grants to support religious foundations and to reward secular officers. State power was fragmented as the class of landed intermediaries grew, and through sub-infeudation the process of fragmentation continued lower down the scale.

The systems of the old Hindu dynasties, in a creaking condition, had already come into their grip.

Udaipur's fate-makers were now no longer the Paramaras. More than three hundred years had already passed since the Paramaras departed from history.

Udaipur's connection now became joined to Chanderi.

quote:
Under the Sultans of Malwa, Bhilsa was one of the provincial capitals of the kingdom in charge of a governor.
Under the Mughals, however, Bhilsa did not enjoy much political importance it being converted into a head-quarter of a small administrative unit. The emperor Aurangzeb renamed the town as Alamgirpur after his own name though it never came into general use. In the 18th century Bhilsa passed into the hands of the Marathas and remained with them since then.

quote:
In all these campaigns the Maratha chiefs, Ranoji Scindia and Malharrao Holkar, had specially distinguished themselves as leaders of great military and political talents which eventually enabled them to carve out principalities for themselves covering almost the whole of the territory of Madhya Bharat.
In 1740 Bajirao died succeeded by his son Balaji as Peshwa who through the agency of the Nizam secured from the Mughal emperor a sort of formal or legal sanction for the otherwise de facto occupation of the Malwa territory by the Marathas through rather an interesting device of getting himself ceremoniously appointed as the emperor's humble Deputy Governor of Malwa. The Maratha chiefs acted as the agents of the Peshwa in the north where they wielded considerable influence in political and military matters. They were besides assigned certain territories within this realm for the maintenance of their troops and for the smooth performance of their duties. The Maratha States of Gwalior, Indore, Dhar and Dewas which covered the whole of Madhya Bharat owe their origin and history to this system.

quote:
The legend regarding this masjid is that the Emperor Aurangzeb, on his return from the Dakhin, passed this place, and seeing this temple, ordered its demolition and the construction of a masjid with its materials. In obedience to his orders the work of demolition was begun by cutting off or otherwise mutilating the sculptured statues that adorn it, and at the present day most of the statues are so mutilated; but at night, the deity of the temple, Mahadeva, appeared to him in a dream, and ordered him on pain of death to desist from his work of demolition, and as an earnest of his threat he would, he said, cause his listener to fall ill. The next morning Aurangzeb found himself ill, and accordingly, afraid of further irritating the deity of the temple, he ordered the stoppage of the work of destruction; vast quantities of gunpowder that had been stored in the temple to blow it up, were taken out and the temple left unharmed, but a masjid was ordered to be erected at the back of the temple, which had been described above, and a mandate of Aurangzeb directed all those who came to pray in the masjid to enter the temple first and having done reverence there to Mahadeva, to enter the masjid.

Whatever the credit attaching to this legend, certain it is that at the present day the temple is frequented by both Hindus and Muhammadans, and the lingam within equally reverenced by both.

quote: उदयपुर को तलाश एक अलेक्ज़ेंडर कनिंघम जैसे नेक इंसान की है, जो भले ही इंजीनियर हो या फौज का अफसर, डॉक्टर हो या टीचर, नेता हो या सचिव, कारोबारी हो या किसान, अलावा हो या दलाल। लेकिन जो जिज्ञासा से भरा हुआ हो और अपने सब दावों से पार जाकर अतीत की आवाज़ खुद भी सुने और दुनिया भर में दूसरों को भी सुनाए।
segments: उदयपुर को तलाश एक अलेक्ज़ेंडर कनिंघम जैसे नेक इंसान की है, जो भले ही इंजीनियर हो या फौज का अफसर, डॉक्टर हो या टीचर, नेता हो या सचिव, कारोबारी हो या किसान, अलावा हो या दलाल। लेकिन जो जिज्ञासा से भरा हुआ हो और अपने सब दावों से पार जाकर अतीत की आवाज़ खुद भी सुने और दुनिया भर में दूसरों को भी सुनाए।
gloss: Udaypur is looking for a good person like Alexander Cunningham, whether engineer or army officer, doctor or teacher, who is full of curiosity and, going beyond his claims, himself hears the voice of the past and makes others hear it too.
note: Udaypur is said to look for a person like Alexander Cunningham, curious and willing to hear the past's voice and share it.

quote: सबसे पहले मेजर जनरल अलेक्जेंडर कनिंघम ने आर्किोलॉजिकल सर्वे ऑफ इंडिया रिपोर्ट, भाग-10, पृष्ठ-83 पर इसका उल्लेख किया। यह 1880 में ही सबसे पहले छपा। प्रसिद्ध इतिहासकार देवदत्त रामकृष्ण भण्डारकर ने प्रोग्रेस रिपोर्ट ऑफ आर्किोलॉजिकल सर्वे वेस्टर्न सर्किल 1913-14 के पृष्ठ-22 पर इस शिलालेख का विवरण दिया है। इसके अलावा एम. बी. गर्दे ने एन्युअल रिपोर्ट ऑफ आर्किोलॉजिकल डिपार्टमेंट इन ग्वालियर स्टेट, संवत् 1974 में इसका जिक्र है।
segments: सबसे पहले मेजर जनरल अलेक्जेंडर कनिंघम ने आर्किोलॉजिकल सर्वे ऑफ इंडिया रिपोर्ट, भाग-10, पृष्ठ-83 पर इसका उल्लेख किया। यह 1880 में ही सबसे पहले छपा। प्रसिद्ध इतिहासकार देवदत्त रामकृष्ण भण्डारकर ने प्रोग्रेस रिपोर्ट ऑफ आर्किोलॉजिकल सर्वे वेस्टर्न सर्किल 1913-14 के पृष्ठ-22 पर इस शिलालेख का विवरण दिया है। इसके अलावा एम. बी. गर्दे ने एन्युअल रिपोर्ट ऑफ आर्किोलॉजिकल डिपार्टमेंट इन ग्वालियर स्टेट, संवत् 1974 में इसका जिक्र है।
gloss: First Major General Alexander Cunningham mentioned it in Archaeological Survey of India Report, part 10, page 83. It was first printed in 1880. Historian D. R. Bhandarkar gave details of this inscription on page 22 of the Progress Report of the Archaeological Survey Western Circle 1913-14. Besides this, M. B. Garde mentions it in the Annual Report of the Archaeological Department in Gwalior State, Samvat 1974.
note: Lists early published notices of the inscription: Cunningham (ASR vol. 10, p. 83, printed 1880), Bhandarkar (Progress Report ASI Western Circle 1913-14, p. 22), and M. B. Garde (Annual Report, Archaeological Dept, Gwalior State, Samvat 1974).
refs: Bhandarkar, Progress Report ASI Western Circle 1913-14, p. 22
Garde, Annual Report of the Archaeological Department, Gwalior State, Samvat 1974

quote: इतिहास के प्रति यह किसी भी संवेदनशील आदमी के लिए बहुत चुभने वाली बेखबरी थी, जिसे देखकर हम दोनों ही दुखी मन से नीचे उतरे और किसी समय चार बुजुर्गों के बीच एक ऊंची सुरक्षा दीवार से घिरे रहे इस राजमहल का चक्कर लगाकर मंदिर की तरफ लौटने लगे। यहां न केंद्र सरकार ने संरक्षण की जरूरत समझी थी और राज्य सरकार के चार संरक्षित स्मारकों में भी यह शामिल नहीं है, यह हमें इस मुहिम में बाद में ज्ञात हुआ।
segments: इतिहास के प्रति यह किसी भी संवेदनशील आदमी के लिए बहुत चुभने वाली बेखबरी थी, जिसे देखकर हम दोनों ही दुखी मन से नीचे उतरे और किसी समय चार बुजुर्गों के बीच एक ऊंची सुरक्षा दीवार से घिरे रहे इस राजमहल का चक्कर लगाकर मंदिर की तरफ लौटने लगे। यहां न केंद्र सरकार ने संरक्षण की जरूरत समझी थी और राज्य सरकार के चार संरक्षित स्मारकों में भी यह शामिल नहीं है, यह हमें इस मुहिम में बाद में ज्ञात हुआ।
gloss: This was a very stinging unawareness of history for any sensitive person; seeing it, we both descended sadly and, circling this palace once enclosed by a high protective wall, started back toward the temple. Neither the central government had felt the need to protect it, nor is it among the state government's four protected monuments; we learnt this later in this campaign.
note: Palace once ringed by a high protective wall; author states neither the Centre nor the state protects it, and it is not among the state's four protected monuments.

segments: उदयपुर में राज्य सरकार के चार स्मारक हैं, जिन पर आने वाला फंड बदस्तूर खर्च होता रहा। कागजों का पेट भी भरता रहा। मगर उदयपुर से उसकी असल जरूरतों के बारे में पूछने की जहमत किसी ने नहीं की।

quote: फंड चार स्मारकों के लिए आता था। लेकिन पांचवे और छठवें की तरफ देखना और उसे भी सूची में शामिल करना बंद दिमाग सरकारी कारिंदों के लिए कृत्र था। फंड जारी करने के पहले किसी ने उदयपुर आकर देखना मुनासिब नहीं समझा कि आधी से ज्यादा रकम एक ही स्मारक पर स्वाहा हो रही है तो इसकी खासियत क्या है और वह खासियत किसे और क्यों नजर आ रही है?
segments: फंड चार स्मारकों के लिए आता था। लेकिन पांचवे और छठवें की तरफ देखना और उसे भी सूची में शामिल करना बंद दिमाग सरकारी कारिंदों के लिए कृत्र था। फंड जारी करने के पहले किसी ने उदयपुर आकर देखना मुनासिब नहीं समझा कि आधी से ज्यादा रकम एक ही स्मारक पर स्वाहा हो रही है तो इसकी खासियत क्या है और वह खासियत किसे और क्यों नजर आ रही है?
gloss: Funds came for four monuments. But looking toward the fifth and sixth and including them in the list was a task beyond closed-minded government functionaries. Before releasing funds no one thought it proper to come to Udaypur and see: if more than half the amount is being consumed on one monument alone, what is its speciality and to whom and why is it visible?
note: Funds came for four monuments, with more than half going to one monument, and nobody visited to see why.

quote: यह आजाद भारत की सरकारों का दोष है कि हमें यह सब उथला भी नहीं पता। भारत के इतिहास, संस्कृति और पुरातत्व विभाग को 15 अगस्त 1947 को टॉप गियर में सक्रिय किया जाना चाहिए था और दुनिया भर के विशेषज्ञों की मदद से हर बरबाद विरासत को सहजने की शुरुआत होनी थी। हर शिलालेख को पढ़ा जाना था।
segments: यह आजाद भारत की सरकारों का दोष है कि हमें यह सब उथला भी नहीं पता। भारत के इतिहास, संस्कृति और पुरातत्व विभाग को 15 अगस्त 1947 को टॉप गियर में सक्रिय किया जाना चाहिए था और दुनिया भर के विशेषज्ञों की मदद से हर बरबाद विरासत को सहजने की शुरुआत होनी थी। हर शिलालेख को पढ़ा जाना था।
gloss: It is the fault of independent India's governments that we do not know even this superficially. India's history, culture and archaeology department should have been activated in top gear on 15 August 1947, and with the help of experts worldwide the saving of every ruined heritage should have begun. Every inscription was to be read.
note: Author's assessment that independent India's governments failed to know or document such heritage; the heritage and archaeology departments should have been activated on 15 August 1947 and every inscription read.

quote: नारायण व्यास, जिन्होंने आर्कियोलॉजिकल सर्वे ऑफ इंडिया (एसआई) में अपनी सेवाएं 1972 में शुरू की थीं और अपनी नौकरी की शुरुआत में सीधे उदयपुर भेजे गए थे। उन्हें अच्छी तरह याद है कि तब मंदिर के तीन तरफ लोगों ने बिल्कुल ही सटकर अपने मकान बना रखे थे। वे कई दशकों पुराने थे। हम सोच भी नहीं सकते कि यह किस हाल में कब से पड़ा रहा होगा। तब उन लोगों को मुआवजा देकर हटाया गया था। तीनों तरफ चार फुट मलबा हटाया तो मंदिर की शानदार बुनियाद बाहर निकली थी, जो आज भी देखी जा सकती है।
segments: नारायण व्यास, जिन्होंने आर्कियोलॉजिकल सर्वे ऑफ इंडिया (एसआई) में अपनी सेवाएं 1972 में शुरू की थीं और अपनी नौकरी की शुरुआत में सीधे उदयपुर भेजे गए थे। उन्हें अच्छी तरह याद है कि तब मंदिर के तीन तरफ लोगों ने बिल्कुल ही सटकर अपने मकान बना रखे थे। वे कई दशकों पुराने थे। हम सोच भी नहीं सकते कि यह किस हाल में कब से पड़ा रहा होगा। तब उन लोगों को मुआवजा देकर हटाया गया था। तीनों तरफ चार फुट मलबा हटाया तो मंदिर की शानदार बुनियाद बाहर निकली थी, जो आज भी देखी जा सकती है।
gloss: Dr. Narayan Vyas, who began his service in the Archaeological Survey of India in 1972 and was sent straight to Udaypur at the start of his job. He remembers well that then people had built their houses completely adjoining the temple on three sides. They were decades old. Then those people were removed after being given compensation. When four feet of debris was removed on all three sides, the splendid foundation of the temple came out, which can be seen even today.
note: Narayan Vyas, posted to Udaypur at start of ASI service in 1972, recalls houses abutting the temple on three sides removed with compensation; clearing four feet of debris revealed the temple's foundation.

quote: जब वे उदयपुर पहुंचे तो खुलासा किया कि 1972 में नीलकंठेश्वर भगवान ने सबसे पहले अपने आसपास की सफाई के लिए ही बुलाया था। उदयपुर में अब वे दूसरी बड़ी सफाई देखने आए थे। आजादी के बाद एसएसआई द्वारा मंदिर को अपनी पनाह में लेने के बाद वह पहला बड़ा काम था, जो दिखाई दिया। लेकिन उसके बाद इतने सालों में उदयपुर की सुध किसी ने नहीं ली थी।

After the ASI took the temple under its shelter after independence, that was the first major work that was visible. But after that, in so many years, no one took care of Udaypur.
note: Vyas says in 1972 the temple first called him to clean its surroundings; after independence and ASI taking the temple in, that was the first major visible work, and no one attended to Udaypur afterwards.

Ancient monuments 300 to 1000 plus years old are never ‘renovated’, only ‘restored’, a distinction that escapes the babus.

quote: Suresh Mishra and I got off at that corner which — hemmed in by lumps and shanties — was Udaipur's wretched little bus stand. A dust-eating, disorderly and ruined three-way junction, in front of which the tar road runs 16 kilometres away to join Ganj Basoda. Ganj Basoda is the nearest railway station and a small commercial town. Udaipur falls in this same tehsil of Vidisha district. The other road of the junction takes a 90-degree turn and goes off 22 kilometres away toward Mandi Bamora, which is another railway station and a small commercial town. On this same road, seven kilometres from Mandi Bamora, is Kurwai, in whose assembly-constituency Udaipur falls.

quote: For so many years after Independence, not a single elected representative of any panchayat felt that this was something that ought to be better looked after. In the government machinery there was no one who would even make a proposal on paper about this place and push it forward. To no schoolteacher either did anything appear that could be taken further somewhere. In none of the citizens' minds did the thought arise that he should take at least some small initiative for Udaipur's perishing wealth. It is possible that some correspondence too had taken place; but it had no effect here. Most of the local people think of nothing besides their own livelihood and farming — even those people whose everyday needs have been fulfilled more than others'.

quote:
The interest of the Indian visitors was only in the temple — not even the temple, but in the Neelkantheshwar Mahadev seated in the sanctum of the temple. People would go straight in, perform worship and ablution (*abhishek*), and, hanging one more category of the poison of their endless desires around the neck of Bholenath [Shiva], come out — a son's job, a daughter's marriage, court matters, land disputes, the wish to become wealthy.

Ever since cameras became easy and ever since the mobile came into hand, people would stop outside for a while to take photos and the like. Very few people would pay attention to the astonishing architecture of the temple. Next to none would peer into its real history. All would come out of the temple and, without wasting time, get out of Udaipur.

gloss: Upadhyay visited Udaypur many times in the last year. He believes that local people have a separate world and their living connection with their priceless heritage has not been such that they take any effective initiative on their own. note: Upadhyay says locals have been distant and indifferent to their heritage; without their involvement outside or government efforts will not yield results.

quote: इतना जरूर है कि अगर इन शिलालेखों के सुंदर और साफ-सुथरे अनुवाद मंदिर के परिसर में ही उपलब्ध होते तो न सिर्फ गांव के लोगों की समझ बेहतर बनाने में मददगार होते बल्कि यहां आने वाले पर्यटकों को भी स्थानीय इतिहास की जानकारी के लिहाज से सिद्ध होते। यह अजीब है कि जब ये शिलालेख पढ़ लिए गए हैं तो इन्हें सरकारी तिजोरियों में क्यों बंद करके रखा हुआ है? यह किसकी मंशा थी कि इन्हें बाहर आम लोगों के लिए न दिखाया जाए और अगर किस्मत से ये कहीं बचे रह गए हैं तो इन पर परदा ही पड़ा रहने दिया जाए। किसी लीडर या किसी अफसर के दिमाग में यह बात कभी क्यों नहीं आई कि मंदिरों, महलों और किलों में पाए शिलालेखों के अनुवाद वहीं लगाए जाने चाहिए और इनकी प्रस्तुति भी बदहाल टीन के टुकड़ों पर घिसे-पिटे तरीके से नहीं होनी चाहिए।

gloss: At least, had clean and good translations of these inscriptions been available in the temple complex, they would have helped improve the understanding of the villagers and been useful to visiting tourists for local history. It is strange that when these inscriptions have been read, they are kept locked in government vaults. Whose intention was it that they not be shown to the public outside, and, if by luck they survive somewhere, that a veil be left on them? Why did it never occur to some leader or officer that translations of inscriptions found in temples, palaces and forts should be put up right there, and their presentation should not be on worn tin pieces in a stale way.
note: Recommends that translations of inscriptions be displayed at the temple itself, for villagers and tourists, and not on worn tin pieces; questions why read inscriptions are locked in government vaults.

gloss: In March 2021 we both met the ASI regional director Dr. P. K. Mishra at his office in Bhopal, and our suggestion was that in the huge temple complex of Udaypur Hindi-English translations of select inscriptions that give tourists new information should be displayed. Now people come. They have darshan. They stroll a little and leave without any information, into nothingness. Besides, the most skilled employees should be posted at such places, who themselves have an interest in raising the lustre of such places. They should not be like the unskilled workers of MNREGA.

gloss: Based on the Udaypur experience he says that if the state government gets panchayats comprehensively documented it will be a big initiative. We are doing this work in 10-12 districts. If the government does this work in all the panchayats of the state, it is certain that many priceless things will come to our notice together for the first time. We shall learn what is of archaeological importance in panchayats and villages.
note: Proposal: state government should have panchayats comprehensively documented, as INTACH is doing in 10-12 districts.

quote: हमने शासन को भी सुझाया है कि प्रदेश और जिला स्तर पर स्कूल-कॉलेजों में हेरिटेज वॉक अनिवार्य की जानी चाहिए। कॉलेज और यूनिवर्सिटी के विद्यार्थी पूरे देश में मौजूद महान विरासत को जाकर देखें। स्कूल की बड़ी कक्षाओं के विद्यार्थी अपने प्रदेश के ऐसे ही स्थानों पर ले जाए जाएं और जिले या ब्लॉक स्तर की धरोहर तक छोटी कक्षाओं के विद्यार्थियों को साल में कम से कम दो बार ले जाया जाए। इसके लिए आसान टूरिस्ट सर्किट का विकास पर्यटन विभाग कर सकता है, जिनमें एक ही दिन में दो-तीन स्मारकों का भ्रमण रूट बनाया जाए। सरकार से लेकर पंचायत तक मंत्री से लेकर एक गांव का पंच तक इसमें सक्रिय योगदान कर सकता है। यह मिशन मोड का काम है, केवल फाइलों का पेट कागजों और ऑर्डरों से भरने का नहीं है।

gloss: We have also suggested to the government that heritage walks should be made compulsory in schools and colleges at state and district level. College and university students should go and see the great heritage present across the country. Senior school students should be taken to such places in their own state, and younger students should be taken to district or block level heritage at least twice a year. For this the tourism department can develop easy tourist circuits with routes covering two or three monuments in one day. From government to panchayat, from a minister to a village panch, everyone can contribute actively. This is mission-mode work, not for filling files with papers and orders.
note: Author's proposal to the government: compulsory heritage walks in schools and colleges, easy tourist circuits with two or three monuments in a day, mission-mode work from minister to village panch.

gloss: This is not just about khasra number 822, the Udaipur palace. It is about giving new life to the whole of Udaipur; otherwise Udaipur will soon cease to exist. I believe all social and business organisations of the district should come together with open hearts and pockets, and give Udaipur one day every month.
note: Argues the issue is not only the palace (khasra no. 822) but renewing the whole of Udaypur, calling on district organisations to give a day each month.

gloss: Organisations that are now awake should shake their elected representatives and take a procession to Udaipur. School and college groups should keep arriving; educational institutions should run constructive campaigns. This work cannot be left to one party.
note: Calls on organisations, school and college groups and educational institutions to take part; the work cannot rest on one party.

gloss: I suggested that every week Udaipur's heritage team take up cleaning these thickets. If we only clean these tangles, Udaipur's clear face can emerge. We should not leave everything to the government. A local phase of the Swachhta Abhiyan could begin here, in which rubbish will not be cleaned but centuries of settled dust removed.
note: Proposal that the heritage team clean the overgrowth weekly, as a local phase of a cleanliness campaign, rather than leave it all to government.

quote: हमारी बेफिक्री तोड़ने के लिए हमारा यहां बार-बार आना अनिवार्य होना चाहिए था। हर स्कूल-कॉलेज के लिए बाध्य होना चाहिए था कि वे अपने हर बच्चे को लगातार यहां लेकर आएं और सवाल करना अनिवार्य हो। उन्हें सवालों के जवाब दिए जाएं और यहां का इतिहास बताएं। इतिहास मतलब आधा-अधूरा सच नहीं, पूरा और असल इतिहास। पहले क्या था और फिर क्या हुआ था, इसकी पूरी डिटेल्स दस्तावेजी सबूतों के साथ उन्हें बताई जाए।
segments: हमारी बेफिक्री तोड़ने के लिए हमारा यहां बार-बार आना अनिवार्य होना चाहिए था। हर स्कूल-कॉलेज के लिए बाध्य होना चाहिए था कि वे अपने हर बच्चे को लगातार यहां लेकर आएं और सवाल करना अनिवार्य हो। उन्हें सवालों के जवाब दिए जाएं और यहां का इतिहास बताएं। इतिहास मतलब आधा-अधूरा सच नहीं, पूरा और असल इतिहास। पहले क्या था और फिर क्या हुआ था, इसकी पूरी डिटेल्स दस्तावेजी सबूतों के साथ उन्हें बताई जाए।
gloss: To break our unconcern, our coming here again and again should have been made compulsory. Every school and college should have been bound to bring each of its children here continuously, and asking questions should be compulsory. Their questions should be answered and the history of this place told. History means not half-baked truth but full and real history. What was there before and what happened later should be told to them in full detail with documentary evidence.
note: Author proposes that schools and colleges bring every child to such sites, with questions answered and documented history told.

quote: क्या वह सिर्फ़ तराशे गए पत्थरों का एक ऐसा मंदिर भर है, जिससे भारत भरा हुआ है और जो भाग्य से बचा रह गया है और अब हम उसके लिए कुछ नहीं कर सकते, जो करना है सिर्फ़ सरकारों को करना है? क्या ये ऐसे स्मारक हैं, जिनसे हम आम लोगों का कोई लेना-देना नहीं है? मुझे लगता है कि उदयपुर हमारे लिए एक अर्थपूर्ण उद्देश्य है। मेरे लिए अपने आसपास की हर ऐसी धरोहर एक बड़ा प्रश्न है और उत्तर भी है।
segments: क्या वह सिर्फ़ तराशे गए पत्थरों का एक ऐसा मंदिर भर है, जिससे भारत भरा हुआ है और जो भाग्य से बचा रह गया है और अब हम उसके लिए कुछ नहीं कर सकते, जो करना है सिर्फ़ सरकारों को करना है? क्या ये ऐसे स्मारक हैं, जिनसे हम आम लोगों का कोई लेना-देना नहीं है? मुझे लगता है कि उदयपुर हमारे लिए एक अर्थपूर्ण उद्देश्य है। मेरे लिए अपने आसपास की हर ऐसी धरोहर एक बड़ा प्रश्न है और उत्तर भी है।
gloss: Is it merely a temple of carved stones, of which India is full, which has survived by luck and for which we can now do nothing, so that only governments must act? Are these monuments with which ordinary people have nothing to do? I think Udaypur is a meaningful purpose for us. For me every such heritage around me is a big question and also an answer.
note: Author asks whether the temple is only carved stone for governments to look after, or something ordinary people share; frames Udaypur as meaningful to residents (community stewardship).

quote:
उदयपुर महान भारत की सांस्कृतिक पहचान का प्रतीक है और अगर यह भाग्य से ही सही बचा रह गया है तो इस अमूल्य धरोहर को उसके मूल रूप में सुरक्षित रखने और सहजने का काम किसी और का नहीं है। वह सिर्फ़ उदयपुर की पंचायत के निवासियों का भी नहीं है। वह इस इलाके के हरেক नागरिक का है।

उदयपुर हमारे सृजनशील महान पूर्वजों की एक ऐसी रचना है, जो आज भी उनसे हमारे संबंध का स्मरण कराती है। वे अनगिनत शिलालेख उस संबंध के ही पत्थरों पर उत्कीर्ण दस्तावेज हैं।
segments:

उदयपुर हमारे सृजनशील महान पूर्वजों की एक ऐसी रचना है, जो आज भी उनसे हमारे संबंध का स्मरण कराती है। वे अनगिनत शिलालेख उस संबंध के ही पत्थरों पर उत्कीर्ण दस्तावेज हैं।
gloss: Udaypur is a symbol of India's great cultural identity; if it has survived by luck, preserving this priceless heritage in its original form is nobody else's task. It does not belong only to the residents of Udaypur's panchayat; it belongs to every citizen of the area. Udaypur is a creation of our creative ancestors that still reminds us of our bond with them. The countless inscriptions are documents engraved on the stones of that bond.
note: Argues preserving the monument is the duty of every citizen of the region, not only Udaypur's panchayat residents; inscriptions as documents of the link with ancestors.

quote: वर्तमान मध्यप्रदेश में 30 से ज्यादा राजे-रजवाड़े रहे होंगे, जो अंग्रेजी हुकूमत के समकालीन हैं। इनकी ज्यादातर विरासत खंडहर में बदल रही है। उसका रखरखाव सही नहीं है। राजाओं के उत्तराधिकारी दूसरे स्थानों पर चले गए हैं। कई जगह वे बचे ही नहीं हैं। ऐसे में इतिहास के अनछुए अध्यायों को विस्तार से जानने के लिए एक सामाजिक अभियान की जरूरत है और इसका सुफल स्थानीय समाज की सक्रिय सहभागिता के बिना संभव नहीं है।

gloss: In present-day Madhya Pradesh there must have been more than 30 kings and princely states contemporary with British rule. Most of their heritage is turning into ruins. Its upkeep is not proper. The successors of the kings have moved to other places. In many places they do not survive. In such a case, to know the untouched chapters of history in detail a social campaign is needed, and its fruit is not possible without the active participation of the local society.
note: Upadhyay: 30-plus princely houses of present-day Madhya Pradesh, much heritage in ruins; untouched chapters need a social campaign that cannot succeed without active local participation.

gloss: For this, high-quality short and detailed publications on local history and archaeology should be made and kept in schools and colleges themselves. Short films should be made and broadcast in the digital world. Our heritage should be made a compulsory central theme in writing and speech competitions among children. Through this they will be eager to read about their history and go and see it.
note: Proposals to connect new generations with heritage: good publications on local history and archaeology kept in schools and colleges, short films, and heritage as a central theme in writing and speech contests.
